content:
A vote
was taken (unanimous) and the altered
motion was carried as follows:

 

“Council notes that:

Every single river in England is now polluted beyond legal
limits, with raw sewage spills from overflows contributing
massively to the pollution of our waterways.
Anglian Water provides sewerage services for our region, and in
2025 the company dumped sewage 16,779 times for a total of 101,598
hours - including 3,512 hours of sewage discharges in local
waterways in South Cambridgeshire.
Our
local rivers - including the River Cam, the River Great Ouse, the
River Mel, the River Granta - are particularly threatened by
further sewage discharges; with many of these being globally
significant chalk stream habitats, containing numerous unique
species and providing a high level of biodiversity in an otherwise
nature depleted area.
High volumes of rainwater entering the sewerage system, as well
as the addition of pollutants from human sources, increases the
risk of overflows and sewage dumping. In addition to sewage,
run-off from farms and wash-off from roads also contribute to river
pollution.
National and local organisations are campaigning to improve our
river quality, demonstrating the significant and growing public
interest in protecting our watercourses.


 

Council believes:

-       
That protecting and improving the quality of our
rivers and chalk streams should be reflected in all relevant
Council policies, decisions and activities.

-       
That the level of sewage discharging at both
local and national level is disgraceful and unacceptable; more so
than ever, taking into account the
cumulative impact of years of sewage dumping and the growing local
impacts of the climate and ecological crises.

-       
That the UK Government should:

-       
Accelerate plans to replace Ofwat with a create a
super-regulator with wider enforcement powers over the economic and
environmental performance of water companies.

-       
Ensure this regulator has sufficient new powers
to prevent sewage dumps, increase inspection regularity of water
companies and farms, and rigorously prosecute
offenders.

-       
Strengthen the Office for Environmental
Protection and provide more funding to the Environment Agency and
Natural England to help protect our rivers and enforce
environmental laws.

-       
Properly fund local and highways authorities so
that they can introduce systems to prevent road pollutants from
entering our waterways.

 

Council further believes that local residents, who
are already facing a cost-of-living crisis, should not bear the
cost of water companies upgrading decades worth of crumbling
infrastructure, while these companies continue to make significant
profits, especially in light of average water bills in our region
being set to rise by 7% this year.

 

Council resolves to:

-       
request that the Leader of the Council and the
Lead Cabinet Member for Environment write to the Secretary of the
State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to make clear the
position of this council and call for tougher action to bring the
practice of sewage dumping to an end.

-       
Request that the Leader of the Council and Lead
Cabinet Member for Environment write to Anglian Water requesting
urgent action to greatly reduce sewage outflows at key sites such
as Haslingfield, Foxton and Whaddon and to provide an update on
progress to date as well as their future
plans.”
topline: The Council has decided to address the issue of sewage dumping in local waterways by calling for tougher action from the UK Government and Anglian Water.

content:
A vote
was taken (unanimous) and the motion was carried as
follows:

 

“Council notes:

Cambridgeshire has among the lowest funding per person for GPs
of anywhere in the country.
Between 2011 and 2021, Cambridge’s population grew by 18%
- triple the national average. South Cambridgeshire is projected to
grow by a further 37% by 2041, with the government pushing for that
to be even higher.
Addenbrooke’s A&E was built for a quarter of the
patients it now receives. It faces an acute care deficit of
approximately 160 beds, and its regional major trauma capacity is
regularly breached. Addenbrooke’s A&E saw 12,280
incidents of patients waiting more than 12 hours before receiving
treatment in the year to November 2025.


 

Council further notes:

That the Government has laid before Parliament the
“Greater Cambridge Development Corporation (Establishment)
Order 2026”, which if approved, will go into effect on 23
July 2026.
The
stated ambition of the Cambridge Growth Company (the predecessor to
the Development Corporation) for growth in Greater Cambridge to be
“infrastructure led”, including health and other social
infrastructure.


 

Council recognises the campaigns being run to
improve healthcare across Cambridgeshire, as spearheaded by our
local MPs, including those putting pressure on the Government to
introduce a right to see a GP in 7 days, calling for fundamental
reform of and investment into NHS dentistry, and calling for urgent
expansion of urgent and emergency care provision.

 

Council resolves to request that the Leader and the
Lead Cabinet Member for Healthy Communities write to the Chair of
the Development Corporation’s Board, once
appointed:

Outlining the importance of delivering new health infrastructure
for both existing and new communities;
Highlighting the concerns residents have raised about the
provision of health infrastructure; and
Inviting the Development Corporation to provide an update to the
Council on its plans to work with the Integrated Care Board to
deliver health infrastructure in Greater Cambridge, for example
through attendance at a future meeting of the Scrutiny and Overview
Committee, subject to that Committee’s
agreement.”
topline: The Council has decided to address the healthcare infrastructure deficit in Cambridgeshire by requesting the Development Corporation to prioritize new health infrastructure for existing and new communities.

content:
By unanimous vote in favour of
the officer recommendation of refusal, the Committee refused the
application for the following reasons:
i.              
The proposed development is located on undeveloped
agricultural land outside the development framework of Linton and
would introduce residential development into the open countryside
in a location that is not justified by its nature or
function.

The proposal would extend development beyond the
development framework of the village in a manner that conflicts
with the established spatial approach to growth, which seeks to
concentrate development within existing settlements. In the absence
of a clear and convincing justification, the development would
represent unjustified encroachment into the countryside and
undermine the plan-led distribution of development. Accordingly,
the proposal is contrary to Policy S/2, S/3, S/6, S/7 and S/9 of
the South Cambridgeshire Local Plan 2018.
ii.             
The proposed development, by virtue of its scale and
siting, would result in a harmful urbanising influence on a
currently open and rural landscape. The site contributes to the
character of the wider area through its openness, field pattern and
visual relationship with the surrounding valley
landscape.

The introduction of built form and associated
infrastructure would erode the rural setting of Linton and diminish
the transition between the village and countryside. The development
would be clearly visible from surrounding public viewpoints,
including elevated positions and local rights of way, leading to
adverse effects on visual amenity.

As a result, the proposal would cause significant
harm to the character and appearance of the landscape. Accordingly,
the proposal is contrary to Policies HQ/1 and NH/2 of the South
Cambridgeshire Local Plan 2018 and the provisions of the National
Planning Policy Framework.
iii.            
The proposed development would result in the
permanent loss of approximately 6.76 hectares of agricultural land
likely to be best and most versatile. This represents a finite and
valuable resource.

In the absence of evidence to demonstrate otherwise,
the proposal would lead to the unjustified loss of higher quality
agricultural land, and no clear justification has been provided to
outweigh this harm arising from the loss of this resource.
Accordingly, the proposal is contrary to Policy NH/3 of the South
Cambridgeshire Local Plan 2018.
iv.           
The proposed development fails to make adequate
provision, through a planning obligation or otherwise, for the
infrastructure required to mitigate the impacts arising from the
development. In particular, no satisfactory mechanism has been
secured to deliver or contribute towards Outdoor Sport and Sports
Facilities. In the absence of such provision, the development would
place additional pressure on existing infrastructure serving
Linton, resulting in an unacceptable deterioration in the quality
and capacity of these facilities.

Furthermore, it has not been demonstrated that the
development would meet the statutory tests for planning
obligations, in that the necessary infrastructure has neither been
secured nor shown to be deliverable in a manner which is necessary,
directly related to the development, and fairly and reasonably
related in scale and kind.

The proposal is therefore contrary to Policy TI/8 of
the South Cambridgeshire Local Plan (2018), the Greater Cambridge
Planning Obligations SPD (2026), and the National Planning Policy
Framework (2024), which require that development is supported by
adequate infrastructure provision to mitigate its
impacts.
v.             
Delegated authority to officers to make minor
amendments to the reasons for refusal.
vi.           
If an appeal is lodged against the decision to
refuse this application, delegated authority to officers to
negotiate and complete the Planning Obligations required in
connection with this development.
topline: The Committee has decided to refuse a proposed residential development on undeveloped agricultural land outside the development framework of Linton.

content:
By unanimous vote in favour of
the officer recommendation of refusal, the Committee refused the
application for the following reasons:
i.              
The proposed residential development site lies
within the designated Green Belt, wherein there is a strong
presumption against inappropriate development. The proposal
constitutes inappropriate development in the Green Belt, which is,
by definition, harmful. No very special circumstances have been
demonstrated that would clearly outweigh the harm to the Green
Belt, including harm by reason of inappropriateness and any other
identified harm.

In addition, the Local Planning Authority cannot
identify a demonstrable housing need that would justify the release
of this Green Belt site, nor has evidence been provided to support
such a need.

As such, the proposal is contrary to the provisions
of the National Planning Policy Framework (in
particular Section 13: Protecting Green Belt land) and
Policies S/4, S/6 and S/7 and paragraphs 143, 154 and 155 of the
NPPF 2024 which seek to protect the Green Belt from inappropriate
development.
ii.             
The site is located outside the development
framework of Stapleford, and on undeveloped, agricultural land
within the countryside.

Policy S/7 of the South Cambridgeshire Local Plan
2018 seeks to direct new development to sites within development
frameworks to protect the countryside from gradual encroachment and
prevent incremental growth in unsustainable locations. Development
outside these frameworks will only be permitted where the site is
allocated within a neighbourhood plan, or is for horticulture,
forestry, outdoor recreation, or other uses which require a
countryside location, or where supported
by other specific policies in the Local Plan.

The proposal would extend development beyond the
development framework of the village in a manner that conflicts
with the established spatial approach to growth, which seeks to
concentrate development within existing settlements.

In the absence of a clear and convincing
justification, the development would represent unjustified
encroachment into the countryside and undermine the plan-led
distribution of development. Accordingly, the proposal is contrary
to Policy S/2, S/3, S/6, S/7 and S/9 of the South Cambridgeshire
Local Plan 2018 and paragraph 187 of the NPPF 2024.
iii.            
The proposed development would result in the loss of
approximately 7.4 hectares of agricultural land which is identified
as Grade 3a and is considered to comprise best and most versatile
agricultural land. This represents a finite and valuable
resource.

Policy NH/3 of the South Cambridgeshire Local Plan
2018 seeks to protect Grades 1, 2 and 3a agricultural land from
irreversible loss unless the land is allocated for development or
it can be demonstrated that sustainability considerations and need
for the development outweigh the need to protect the agricultural
value of the land.

The site is not allocated for development and it has not been demonstrated that
the sustainability benefits of the proposal or need for the
development would outweigh the harm arising from the loss of this
agricultural resource. The proposal would therefore result in the
irreversible loss of the best and most versatile agricultural land.
In the absence of evidence to demonstrate otherwise, the proposal
would lead to the unjustified loss of higher quality agricultural
land, and no clear justification has been provided to outweigh this
harm arising from the loss of this resource.

Accordingly, the proposal is contrary to Policy NH/3
of the South Cambridgeshire Local Plan 2018 and paragraph 187 of
the NPPF 2024.
iv.           
Delegated authority to officers to make minor
amendments to the reasons for refusal.
v.             
If appeal is lodged against the decision to refuse
this application, delegated authority to the Director of Planning
to negotiate and complete the Planning Obligations required in
connection with this development and review the reasons for refusal
in light of any further information
submitted with any appeal.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to refuse a proposed residential development on Green Belt land due to lack of very special circumstances, failure to demonstrate housing need, and conflict with local planning policies.

purpose:
1.    
The purpose of this report is to set out the results
of the referendum on the Heydon Neighbourhood Plan and make a
recommendation to Council on whether the Neighbourhood Plan should
be formally made (adopted) by South Cambridgeshire District Council
(SCDC).
 
Background
 

2.    
The Heydon Neighbourhood Area was designated on 15
March 2024. The neighbourhood area is for the whole area of the
parish areas of Heydon. 
 

3.    
Officers recognise the hard work of those in the
Neighbourhood Plan Working Group and Parish Council have put into
preparing the Plan. Both have strived to ensure that the whole
village have had their opportunity to have an input into the final
Plan.
 

4.    
A Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) and
Habitats Regulations Assessment (HRA) screening was undertaken on a
draft version of the Neighbourhood Plan, and a screening
determination was published in April 2025.
 

5.    
Pre-submission public consultation on the draft
Neighbourhood Plan was undertaken by the Parish Council from 9 May
2025 until 20 June 2025. Officers provided a formal response to the
consultation, providing constructive comments about the
Neighbourhood Plan to assist the neighbourhood plan group with
finalising the Neighbourhood Plan. Officers met with the steering
group to discuss these comments, and the submission version of the
plan took on board many of the suggested changes.
 

6.    
On 1 December 2025 Heydon Parish Council submitted
their Neighbourhood Plan to SCDC. Officers confirmed by carrying
out a Legal Compliance Check for the Neighbourhood Plan that the
submitted version of the Neighbourhood Plan and its accompanying
supporting documents complied with all the relevant statutory
requirements at this stage of plan making. We therefore were able
to carry out a consultation on the Heydon Neighbourhood Plan from
15 December 2025 to 9 February 2026. This extended period of
consultation was to take into account
that the consultation period extended over the Christmas holiday
period. We wished to ensure everyone had an opportunity to comment
on the Plan.
 

7.    
Officers, in conjunction with Heydon Parish Council,
appointed an independent examiner to consider this Neighbourhood
Plan. The examiner appointed to undertake the
examination of a Neighbourhood Plan: must be independent of both
the District Council and Parish Council; cannot be the same
examiner that undertakes a health check of the Neighbourhood Plan;
and must not have any interest in any land that may be affected by
the Neighbourhood Plan. The examiner appointed was Andrew
Ashcroft. On 24 February 2026 the Neighbourhood Plan, its
accompanying supporting documents and all comments submitted during
the public consultation on the submission version of the
Neighbourhood Plan were provided to the examiner with a request for
him to carry out the examination on the Neighbourhood
Plan.
 

8.    
The examiner issued on 2 March 2026 a note which set
out the arrangements for the examination, and on the 9 March 2026 a
clarification note which included some questions for the Parish
Council. The Parish Council responded to the questions set for them
on 20 March 2026.
 

9.    
The Examiner’s Report was received on 18 May
2026. The examiner in his report concludes that subject to a series
of recommended modifications the Heydon Neighbourhood Plan meets
all the necessary legal requirements and should proceed to
referendum. The examiner also recommended that the referendum
should be held within the neighbourhood area only (recommending
that that the Plan should proceed to
referendum based on the neighbourhood area as approved by the
District Council on 15 March 2024).
 

10. 
Once the Examiner’s Report was received, the
Council was able to consider the conclusions of the
Examiner’s Report, and whether those conclusions should be
acted upon and therefore that the Neighbourhood Plan should proceed
to referendum. This included considering whether the
examiner’s recommended modifications to the Neighbourhood

2.

and referendum have to be initially met

examination and a referendum date has been set. Officers will

opportunity.

formally ‘made’ (adopted) by the Council, the Joint

recommendation to Council, in consultation with the Lead Member for

otherwise compatible with, EU obligations, including Human Rights.
Included as part of the

Neighbourhood Plan in relation to the ‘protected
characteristics’ as identified in the Equality Act 2010. The

adults; the policies or proposals contained within the

or discrimination in the Plan area and the Neighbourhood Plan does
not raise any issues in relation to any of the convention rights in
the Human Rights Act 1998. The Examiner agreed with this
assessment.

the preparation of the Neighbourhood Plan. Policy HEY13 promotes
sustainable transport, seeking to protect and enhance the existing
public rights of way network in the parish, ensuring that
development proposals mitigate or reduce any adverse visual impacts
where development proposals would be visible from a public right of
way. Policy HEY7 takes a proactive approach to mitigating and
adapting to climate change, ensuring that proposals coming forward

demonstrate sustainable use of resources and high energy efficiency

On 15
April 2026 a nomination was received from Harston Parish Council in
respect of The Queens Head Public House, 48 Royston Road, Harston,
Cambridge, CB22 7NH. This is a re-nomination of an asset that was
removed from the list on 28 January 2026 in accordance with the
legislation following expiry of the listing.
 
Following consideration of the nomination, Notices of Nomination
were sent to ward members, Cllr Ariel Cahn, Cllr Dr Lisa Redrup and
Cllr Michael Atkins (for the district Ward of Harston and
Comberton), to the Parish Council acknowledging their nomination
and to the owners and occupiers. The nomination was publicised
through the Council’s parish e-bulletin, and the Lead Member
for Communities was notified. Due to local government elections
taking place during the 8 week decision making period, Cllr Atkins
ceased to be an elected member and a Notice of Nomination was sent
to newly elected ward member, Cllr Laurence
Damary-Homan.

Officers have considered the nomination along with the feedback
received following issue of Notices of Nomination and are satisfied
that the non-ancillary and current use of the asset as detailed in
the nomination form and accompanying map does further the social
well-being, or cultural recreational or sporting interests of the
local community.  It is also considered
realistic to think there can continue to be non-ancillary use of
the asset which will further the social interests of the local
community. Therefore, it can be accepted onto the Council’s
list of Assets if Community Value, in accordance with Section 88
(1) of the Localism Act 2011.

The
Queens Head Public House provides clear and demonstratable social
value to the community of Harston and neighbouring
villages.
 
The
evidence provided, including community testimonials, demonstrates
that the property is used in a manner which furthers the social
wellbeing and social interests of the local community. The Queens
Head performs an important role as a community meeting place,
providing a valued and accessible environment where residents can
gather, interact, and maintain social connections. It is used to
celebrate important family events such as wedding anniversaries and
large family gatherings. It is used for informal business meetings
and noted to be very welcoming to those with disabilities making
accommodations to assist with ease of use.
 
Testimonial evidence indicates that the pub is a key venue for
informal socialising, contributing to community cohesion and
helping to reduce social isolation. A recent singing event held at
the pub bought together residents, reflecting the community spirit
of the village.
 
In
addition to its function as a public house and restaurant, the
asset offers inclusive facilities that broaden its community value,
including a safe and secure children’s play area which
supports family use of the premises, and a welcoming approach to
well behaved dogs, enabling a wider cross section of the community
to attend. These features strengthen its role as a space for shared
community activity and interaction.
It is
realistic to think that such use can continue in the
future.
 
Taken
together, these functions demonstrate that the non ancillary use of the asset furthers the social
wellbeing and social interests of the local community and continues
to meet the definition of an Asset of Community Value.

The
options are:
(a) To
accept the nomination and place the asset on the register of assets
of community value.
(b) To
refuse the nomination and place the asset on the register of
unsuccessful nominations.
topline: The Communications and Communities Service Manager has decided to include The Queens Head Public House as an asset of community value on the Council's register.

aligns with local planning policies, supports sustainable
development, secures essential mitigation measures and addresses
potential impacts on South Cambridgeshire’s communities and
environment. This is the first formal step towards the Development
Consent Order Examination period.
SCDC
considers that the Applicant has met the basic legal requirements
for Consultation, however the Cover Letter raises ongoing concern
about the Applicant’s pre-application engagement with the
Council prior to submission.

purpose:
Purpose 
 

The
purpose of this report is to consider the conclusions of the
Examiner’s Report on the Heydon Neighbourhood Plan,
and whether those conclusions should be acted upon and therefore
that the Neighbourhood Plan should proceed to referendum.
This includes considering whether the examiner’s recommended
modifications to the Neighbourhood Plan should be made, and whether
the Council agrees that the Neighbourhood Plan meets the Basic
Conditions. 

 

Cabinet agreed at its meeting on 26 July 2018 that where the
examiner has concluded that the Neighbourhood Plan is legally
compliant, meets the Basic Conditions (with or without
modifications), and should proceed to referendum, the
Director of Planning has delegated authority to make the
decision on the way forward, in consultation with the Planning Lead
Member. 

 

Background 
 
 

The
Heydon Neighbourhood Area was designated on 15
March 2024. The neighbourhood area is for the whole parish of
Heydon. 


 
 

Officers recognise the hard work of those in
the Neighbourhood
Plan Working Group and Parish Council have put
into put into preparing the
Plan. Both have strived to ensure that the whole
village have their opportunity to have an input into the final
Plan.  

 

A
Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) and Habitats Regulations
Assessment (HRA) screening was undertaken on a draft version of the
Neighbourhood Plan, and a screening determination was published
in April 2025.  

 

Pre-submission public consultation on the draft Neighbourhood
Plan was undertaken by the Parish Council from 9
May 2025 until 20 June 2025. Officers provided a
formal response to the consultation, providing constructive
comments about the plan to assist the Parish Council with
finalising the Neighbourhood Plan. Officers have met with the
Parish Council to discuss these comments and are aware that the
submission version of the plan has taken on board many of the
suggested changes.   

 

On
1 December 2025, Heydon Parish
Council submitted their Neighbourhood Plan to South
Cambridgeshire District Council. Officers have confirmed, as set
out in the Legal Compliance Check for the Neighbourhood Plan, that
the submitted version of the Neighbourhood Plan and its
accompanying supporting documents comply with all the
relevant statutory requirements at this stage of plan making. The
Neighbourhood Plan and its accompanying supporting documents are
published on our website.   

 

Officers, in conjunction with Heydon Parish Council,
appointed an independent examiner to consider this Neighbourhood
Plan. The examiner appointed to undertake the examination of a
Neighbourhood Plan must be: independent of both the District
Council and Parish Council; cannot be the same examiner that
undertakes a health check of the Neighbourhood Plan; and must not
have any interest in any land that may be affected by the
Neighbourhood Plan. The examiner appointed was Andrew Ashcroft.
On 24 February 2026 the Neighbourhood
Plan, its supporting documents and all
comments submitted during the public consultation on the
submission version of the Neighbourhood Plan were provided to the
examiner with a request for him to carry out the examination on the
Neighbourhood Plan.   

 

The
examiner issued on 2 March 2026 a note which set out
the arrangements for the examination and on
the 9 March 2026 issued a clarification note
which included some questions for the Parish Council (PC). The PC
responded to the questions set for them on the 20 March
2026. 

 

The
Examiner’s Report was received by South
Cambridgeshire District Council on 18
May 2026 (see Appendix 1). The examiner in his report
concluded that subject to a series of recommended modifications the
Heydon Neighbourhood Plan met all the necessary legal
requirements and should proceed to referendum. He
also recommends that the referendum should be held within the
neighbourhood area only. 

 

Now
that the Examiner’s Report has been received, the
Council is required to consider the conclusions of the
Examiner’s Report, and whether those conclusions should be
acted upon and therefore that the Neighbourhood Plan
should proceed to referendum. This includes considering
whether the examiner’s recommended modifications to the
Neighbourhood Plan should be made, and whether the Council agrees
that the Neighbourhood Plan meets the Basic Conditions. The Council
must publish its decision in a decision
statement. 

 

Considerations   
 
 

Where

met.

evidence or fact, or a different view is taken by the Council as to
a particular fact, including that the Council is unable to confirm
that the Basic Conditions have been met.

decision on the Examiner’s Report and whether the

weeks of receipt of the report (unless an alternative longer

Council).

reasons set out in the following paragraphs of this decision
statement. Officers agree with the examiner’s conclusions,

referendum, a Neighbourhood Plan must meet a number
of tests known as the ‘Basic Conditions’. The
Basic Conditions are set out in national planning regulations and
are summarised as follows: 


having
regard to national policies and advice contained in guidance issued
by the Secretary of State it is appropriate to make the

the
making of the Neighbourhood Plan contributes to the achievement of
sustainable development. 


the
making of the neighbourhood development plan would not result in
the development plan for the area of the authority proposing that
less housing is provided by means of development taking
place in that area than if the neighbourhood development plan were
not to be made.  


the
making of the Neighbourhood Plan does not breach, and is otherwise
compatible with, EU obligations; and 


prescribed conditions are met in relation to the Neighbourhood
Plan, including that the making of the neighbourhood plan is not
likely to have a significant effect on a European wildlife site or
a European offshore marine site either alone or in combination with
other plans or projects.

advice, it should be noted that an updated version of the National
Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) was published on 12 December 2024.

updates implement both Sections 98 section 99 of the Levelling-up
and Regeneration Act 2023. As a result, an Addendum to the
original Basic Conditions Statement was prepared by Heydon Parish
Council that was consulted on between 15 December 2025 to 9
February 2026.

how the Neighbourhood Plan does

development in accordance with Paragraph 8 of Schedule 4B

Regeneration Act. The Council submitted comments to

process. The examination concluded the following Monday

also meet a number of legal requirements, such as whether
the Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared by a qualifying body and
meets the definition and scope of a Neighbourhood
Plan.

examiner concludes in the executive Summary and
Chapter 8 (see Appendix 1) that subject to a series of recommended
modifications the Heydon Neighbourhood Plan meets the Basic
Conditions and all the necessary legal requirements. The issues he

change the role or purpose of the Neighbourhood Plan; they have
been recommended by the examiner to provide clarity and
precision.

reviewed the examiner’s conclusions and recommended
modifications, and officers and the Parish Council have agreed each

Heydon Parish Council, and

national planning guidance which states that minor (non-material)
updates to a Neighbourhood Plan that would not materially affect

consultation or examination (see National Planning Practice
Guidance, Paragraph 085, Reference ID:

content:
The
purpose of this decision is to decide whether the land/building
nominated should be included as an asset of community value
(“ACV”) on the Council’s register of
ACVs.
 
On 19
March 2026 a nomination was received from Litlington Parish Council
in respect of The Crown Public House, Church Street, Litlington, Nr
Royston, SG8 0QB. This is a re-nomination of an asset that was
removed from the list on 06 April 2026 in accordance with the
legislation following expiry of the listing.
 
Following consideration of the nomination, Notice of Nomination
was sent to Cllr Susan Van de Ven, (at the time, the elected member
for the district Ward of Bassingbourn), to the Parish Council
acknowledging their nomination and to the owners and occupier. The
nomination was publicised through the Council’s parish
e-bulletin and the Lead Member for Communities was
notified.
 
Following South Cambridgeshire District Council elections held
on 7 May 2026, some elected members and/or their roles have
changed.  This decision notice will be
sent to all new and relevant elected members.

Officers have considered the nomination along with the feedback
received following issue of Notices of Nomination and are satisfied
that the non-ancillary use of the asset as detailed in the
nomination form and accompanying map did further the social
well-being or cultural recreational or sporting interests of the
local Community in the recent past.  It
is also considered realistic to think that there is a time in the
next five years when there could be non-ancillary use of the asset
that would further (whether or not in the same way as before) the
social well-being or social interests of the local community.
Therefore, it can be accepted onto the Council’s list of
Assets if Community Value, in accordance with Section 88 (2) of the
Localism Act 2011.

The
nomination demonstrates that the asset has historically played a
significant and multifaceted role in furthering the social
wellbeing and social interests of the local community.
 
Evidence provided shows that, prior to its closure during the
Covid-19 pandemic,
the pub
has been described as the longstanding “hub” of the
village, with a history of hosting charitable events, supporting
community functions, and providing a venue for social interaction.
It has facilitated gatherings for residents of all ages and
backgrounds, contributing to community cohesion and reducing social
isolation, particularly through accessible and informal
opportunities to meet.
 
Further
evidence highlights the role of the public house over several
decades as a focal point for village life, including hosting
entertainment such as live music, quiz nights, bingo and other
social events, alongside hosting weekly meetings and
clubs.
Some
activities that were run supported fundraising for local charities
and community groups and have strengthened the village’s
identity and sense of community.
The
loss of the asset since its closure has been noted as having a
negative impact on opportunities for social interaction within the
village. Its absence is identified as leaving a gap in the range of
facilities available to support community cohesion and
wellbeing.
 
Supporting representations also emphasise the importance of the
asset within the context of a small rural community, where
maintaining accessible spaces for social interaction is
particularly important. Village residents showed overwhelming
support for the pub being maintained as an asset of community
value.
 
Although the property has not been in operation since the
Covid-19 pandemic, it is currently being marketed as a public
house.
 
This
indicates that the lawful use has not been abandoned and that there
remains a realistic prospect that the asset could resume its former
non-ancillary use, thereby continuing to further the social
wellbeing and social interests of the local community.
 
Taken
together, this evidence demonstrates that the non-ancillary use of
the asset has historically furthered the social wellbeing and
interests of the community and that it is realistic to consider
that such use could continue or resume in the future.
 
It
should be noted that in keeping with the Council’s normal
practice, once re-listed the asset will re-enter the Protected
Period that formerly applied, assuming the owner remains the
same.  The Protected Period will
continue until the same end date as before (10/03/2027) or until a
relevant disposal takes place, whichever is the sooner. 

The
options are:
a.    
To accept the nomination and place the asset on the
register of assets of community value.
b.    
To refuse the nomination and place the asset on the
register of unsuccessful nominations.
topline: The Communications and Communities Service Manager has decided to include The Crown Public House as an asset of community value on the Council's register.

The
purpose of this decision is to decide whether the land/building
nominated should be included as an asset of community value
(“ACV”) on the Council’s register of
ACVs.
 
On 27
February 2026 a nomination was received from Heydon Parish Council
in respect of King William IV Public House, 43 Chishill Road,
Heydon, Cambridgeshire, SG8 8PN. This is a re-nomination of an
asset that is due to be removed from the list on 05 May 2026 in
accordance with the legislation following expiry of the
listing.
 
Following consideration of the nomination, Notice of Nomination
was sent to Cllr Dr James Hobro (for the district Ward of Foxton),
to the Parish Council acknowledging their nomination and to the
owners, occupier and leaseholder. The nomination was publicised
through the Council’s parish e-bulletin and the Lead Member
for Communities was notified.

Officers have considered the nomination along with the feedback
received following issue of Notices of Nomination and are satisfied
that the non-ancillary and current use of the asset as detailed in
the nomination form and accompanying map does further the social
well-being, or cultural recreational or sporting interests of the
local community.  It is also considered
realistic to think there can continue to be non-ancillary use of
the asset which will further the social interests of the local
community. Therefore, it can be accepted onto the Council’s
list of Assets if Community Value, in accordance with Sections 88
(1) of the Localism Act 2011.


The King
William IV Public House is the only remaining public house in
the village of Heydon. The premises has recently changed ownership,
having successfully operated through the COVID-19 lockdown period,
and has since been refurbished. The site includes separate external
overnight bed-and-breakfast accommodation, which is of benefit to
local residents requiring space for
visiting friends and family, and provides convenient accommodation
for visitors to the nearby Imperial War Museum Duxford. In
addition, on-site rooms are available for staff
accommodation.

 

The public house performs an important role as a
social hub for the village. Other than the parish church, it
represents the only communal meeting space available in Heydon and
is therefore of significant importance to the parish and its
residents. The premises welcomes both families and dog
owners.

 

Prior to the recent refurbishment, the pub regularly
hosted community and cultural events, including quiz nights,
performances by local musicians, open mic nights (including an
event held on 9 March 2024), and the screening of national sporting
events such as the 2024 Rugby Six Nations Championship. The pub has
also historically provided first employment opportunities for many
young adults in the village, which is particularly important given
the limited availability of public transport. It is envisaged that
these benefits will continue post-refurbishment.


Strong local support for the continued operation of the public
house has been demonstrated through testimonials submitted in
support of the nomination, reflecting the community’s desire
to retain this key village facility.

 
It
meets the description of an asset of community value.

The
options are:
a.    
To accept the nomination and place the asset on the
register of assets of community value.
b.    
To refuse the nomination and place the asset on the
register of unsuccessful nominations.

purpose:
Purpose

 

1.   
The purpose of this report is to agree the Greater
Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 to be published on the
Greater Cambridge Shared Planning Service website. The register
will comprise a spreadsheet (Appendix 1 of this decision) and
accompanying spatial data.

 

2.   
The Cabinet Member for Planning and Transport at
Cambridge City Council is also being asked to agree the Greater
Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 via a parallel
decision.

 

Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register and
national guidelines

 

3.   
The government’s 
Planning Practice Guidance sets
out clear parameters for the compilation and publication of
brownfield land registers.

 

4.   
The purpose of brownfield land registers is to
provide up-to-date and consistent information on sites that local
authorities consider to be appropriate for residential development
having regard to the criteria set out in 
national regulations. Registers
should be published locally as open data and will provide
transparent information about suitable and available
sites.

 

5.   

National regulations require local
planning authorities in England to prepare, maintain and publish
registers of previously developed (brownfield) land. Previously
developed land is defined in 
Annex 2 of the National Planning Policy
Framework. Previously developed
land is also referred to as brownfield land.

 

6.   
Brownfield land registers can contain two parts.
Part 1 comprises all brownfield sites that a local planning
authority has assessed as appropriate for residential development.
This will include sites with extant full or outline planning
permission, prior approval permissions, allocations in the adopted
Local Plans and Area Action Plans, sites with permission in
principle and other sites considered suitable for residential
development. Part 2 is a subset of Part 1 and comprises only those
sites in Part 1 where the local planning authority has decided that
the land would be suitable for a grant of permission in principle
for residential development. The Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land
Register does not include a Part 2, as no sites were identified in
the register where it was deemed appropriate to grant permission in
principle.

 

7.   
Sites should be included in the register where they
are at least 0.25 hectares in area or are capable of supporting at
least five dwellings. Sites must also be suitable and available for
residential development. Residential development of the land must
be considered achievable (within 15 years). Local planning
authorities should also have regard to the development plan,
national policies and advice, and any guidance issued by the
Secretary of State.

 

8.   
Local planning authorities are not required to
undertake consultation in relation to sites they propose to include
only in Part 1 of registers. However, they are required to review
and update the register at least annually.

 

9.   
The information to be included in brownfield land
registers is set out in 
national regulations. The format
requirements are set out in the 
brownfield land register data
standard published by the Ministry
of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Local planning
authorities are encouraged to publish their Register in this format
to enable compliance with requests for information issued by the
Secretary of State.

 

10.  The
Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register has been compiled in
line with 
Planning Practice Guidance. It
contains details of over 100 sites in Cambridge and over 150 sites
in South Cambridgeshire, that have planning permission or are
allocations in the adopted plans. The previous registers have been
reviewed. Existing entries have been amended as appropriate to
reflect development activity on these sites. Recent planning
decisions have been examined to identify new entries for the
register. Where planning permissions have lapsed or been built they
are not removed from the register, however a date is entered in the
‘End date’ column to signify that the permission is
considered closed.

 

11.  The
Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register contains two registers.
One covers Cambridge and the other covers South Cambridgeshire.
They will be published as separate spreadsheets to comply with
government requirements.

 

Next Steps

 

12. 
Once agreed by the Cabinet Member for Planning at
South Cambridgeshire District Council and the Cabinet Member for
Planning and Transport at Cambridge City Council, the
Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 will
be published on the Greater Cambridgeshire Shared Planning
Service 
website.
content:
Purpose

 

1.   
The purpose of this report is to agree the Greater
Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 to be published on the
Greater Cambridge Shared Planning Service website. The register
will comprise a spreadsheet (Appendix 1 of this decision) and
accompanying spatial data.

 

2.   
The Cabinet Member for Planning and Transport at
Cambridge City Council is also being asked to agree the Greater
Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 via a parallel
decision.

 

Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register and
national guidelines

 

3.   
The government’s 
Planning Practice Guidance sets
out clear parameters for the compilation and publication of
brownfield land registers.

 

4.   
The purpose of brownfield land registers is to
provide up-to-date and consistent information on sites that local
authorities consider to be appropriate for residential development
having regard to the criteria set out in 
national regulations. Registers
should be published locally as open data and will provide
transparent information about suitable and available
sites.

 

5.   

National regulations require local
planning authorities in England to prepare, maintain and publish
registers of previously developed (brownfield) land. Previously
developed land is defined in 
Annex 2 of the National Planning Policy
Framework. Previously developed
land is also referred to as brownfield land.

 

6.   
Brownfield land registers can contain two parts.
Part 1 comprises all brownfield sites that a local planning
authority has assessed as appropriate for residential development.
This will include sites with extant full or outline planning
permission, prior approval permissions, allocations in the adopted
Local Plans and Area Action Plans, sites with permission in
principle and other sites considered suitable for residential
development. Part 2 is a subset of Part 1 and comprises only those
sites in Part 1 where the local planning authority has decided that
the land would be suitable for a grant of permission in principle
for residential development. The Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land
Register does not include a Part 2, as no sites were identified in
the register where it was deemed appropriate to grant permission in
principle.

 

7.   
Sites should be included in the register where they
are at least 0.25 hectares in area or are capable of supporting at
least five dwellings. Sites must also be suitable and available for
residential development. Residential development of the land must
be considered achievable (within 15 years). Local planning
authorities should also have regard to the development plan,
national policies and advice, and any guidance issued by the
Secretary of State.

 

8.   
Local planning authorities are not required to
undertake consultation in relation to sites they propose to include
only in Part 1 of registers. However, they are required to review
and update the register at least annually.

 

9.   
The information to be included in brownfield land
registers is set out in 
national regulations. The format
requirements are set out in the 
brownfield land register data
standard published by the Ministry
of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Local planning
authorities are encouraged to publish their Register in this format
to enable compliance with requests for information issued by the
Secretary of State.

 

10.  The
Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register has been compiled in
line with 
Planning Practice Guidance. It
contains details of over 100 sites in Cambridge and over 150 sites
in South Cambridgeshire, that have planning permission or are
allocations in the adopted plans. The previous registers have been
reviewed. Existing entries have been amended as appropriate to
reflect development activity on these sites. Recent planning
decisions have been examined to identify new entries for the
register. Where planning permissions have lapsed or been built they
are not removed from the register, however a date is entered in the
‘End date’ column to signify that the permission is
considered closed.

 

11.  The
Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register contains two registers.
One covers Cambridge and the other covers South Cambridgeshire.
They will be published as separate spreadsheets to comply with
government requirements.

 

Next Steps

 

12. 
Once agreed by the Cabinet Member for Planning at
South Cambridgeshire District Council and the Cabinet Member for
Planning and Transport at Cambridge City Council, the
Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 will
be published on the Greater Cambridgeshire Shared Planning
Service 
website.

That
the Cabinet Member for Planning agrees:
a.    
The Greater Cambridge Brownfield Register -
spreadsheet (Appendix 1 of this decision) and accompanying spatial
data - to be published on the Greater Cambridge Shared Planning
Service website.
b.    
To delegate any further minor editing changes to the
Joint Director for Planning to ensure consistency of approach
between the two Brownfield Registers.

Publication of the Greater Cambridge Brownfield Register is a
requirement under national Planning Practice Guidance and the Town
and Country Planning (Brownfield Land Register) Regulations
2017.

Option:
To not publish the Greater Cambridge Brownfield
Register.
 
Reason
for Rejection: Government requires that local planning authorities
review, update and publish their brownfield land register at least
annually.
topline: The Lead Cabinet member for Planning has decided to publish the Greater Cambridge Brownfield Land Register 2025 on the Greater Cambridge Shared Planning Service website.

content:
Cabinet
has approved the following recommendations:
 

Significant considerations

Grant categories

a.    
Retain the existing number of themes but amend the wording of the
categories to ‘carbon emission reduction or locking up
carbon’ and ‘community engagement on climate change
and/or nature’.

Grant funding limits

a.    To
increase maximum grant limits in line with inflation from
£15,000 to £19,500 but put more of an emphasis on match
funding in communications.

b.   Move from a
70:30 to a 50:50 split between carbon reduction projects and
community engagement/nature projects.

Eligibility criteria

a.   Define the
criteria for community groups better to allow for a clearer
distinction between who is and is not eligible
including:

i. Clarity that projects on school sites/Parent
Teacher Associations (PTA) (excluding school buildings) are
eligible so long as the activity has a benefit in the wider
community.

ii.  Clarity that sports
groups (e.g. bowls clubs) are eligible if they provide benefits to
the wider community such as tackling mental health or strengthening
community ties.

b.    
Amend and strengthen the eligibility checks (i.e. Disclosure
Barring Service (DBS), unspent convictions, planning secured or
demonstrably in progress ahead of submission).

c.  Remove criteria that
excludes applicants from applying for EV charging
infrastructure.

Minor considerations

Grant timing

a.    Formally
introduce a “1-year post-completion update” requirement
to report on agreed project outcomes to capture longer term impact
and outcomes (especially relevant to biodiversity/nature
projects).

purpose:
Purpose
 
1.   
The purpose of this decision is:

 

a.   
To agree the Greater Cambridge Housing Trajectory
and Housing Land Supply Report (Appendix 1 of this decision) to be
published on the Councils’ shared planning service website.
The Greater Cambridge housing trajectory and housing land supply
calculations have been prepared jointly with Cambridge City
Council, consistent with the adopted Local Plans.
 

b.   
To delegate any further minor editing changes to the
Greater Cambridge Housing Trajectory and Housing Land Supply Report
to the Joint Director for Planning where they are technical
matters.
 

Greater Cambridge Housing Trajectory and Housing
Land Supply
 
2.   
National planning policy requires all local planning
authorities with an adopted plan of more than five years old to
identify and update annually a supply of specific deliverable sites
sufficient to deliver a minimum of five years’ worth of
housing against their local housing need calculated using the
standard method. National planning policy also sets out a
requirement to provide a buffer of 5% or 20%, depending on historic
housing delivery.
 
3.   
The Greater Cambridge housing trajectory is used by
Cambridge City Council and South Cambridgeshire District Council to
calculate their housing land supply and also to show anticipated
housing delivery against their housing requirement in the adopted
Local Plans. The Councils have prepared the Greater Cambridge
housing trajectory and five-year supply calculations based on
national planning policy and guidance for housing trajectories,
five-year supply calculations, and the standard method for
calculating local housing need.
 
4.   
The housing land supply for Greater Cambridge has
been calculated:

a.   
based on their local housing need (from the standard
method, published by the Government in December 2024), as the
adopted Local Plans are now more than five years old,

b.   
jointly for Greater Cambridge, as set out in the
adopted Local Plans, and

c.    
with a 5% buffer, as set out in national planning
policy.
 
5.   
The Greater Cambridge housing trajectory and housing
land supply calculations show that jointly for Greater Cambridge,
the Councils have 5.6 years of housing land supply for the
2026-2031 period. The Councils have taken a robust and conservative
approach to assessing the deliverability and / or developability of
each of the sites in the Greater Cambridge housing
trajectory.
 
6.   
National planning policy and guidance sets out the
circumstances where planning policies should be considered out of
date when making decisions on planning applications, and this
includes where the Council cannot demonstrate a five-year housing
land supply. On the basis of the housing land supply calculations
in the Greater Cambridge Housing Trajectory and Housing Land Supply
Report (which is Appendix 1 of this decision), this does not apply
to Cambridge or South Cambridgeshire, as the Councils jointly have
5.6 years of housing land supply.
 
7.   
The Cambridge Local Plan 2018 sets a housing
requirement of 14,000 homes to be delivered between 2011 and 2031.
The new housing trajectory shows that 13,842 dwellings are expected
to be delivered in Cambridge between 2011 and 2031, based on
current information on anticipated phasing and delivery of sites.
The South Cambridgeshire Local Plan 2018 sets a housing requirement
of 19,500 dwellings to be delivered between 2011 and 2031. The new
housing trajectory shows that 24,257 dwellings are expected to be
delivered in South Cambridgeshire between 2011 and 2031, based on
current information on anticipated phasing and delivery of sites.
Together the Local Plans set a housing requirement of 33,500 homes
between 2011 and 2031 for Greater Cambridge. The new housing
trajectory shows that 38,099 dwellings are expected to be delivered
between 2011 and 2031. The Councils have already started preparing
a new Greater Cambridge Local Plan, and as part of this the
Councils are considering the appropriate level of housing need for
Greater Cambridge, along with where development should be located
and the specific sites to deliver new homes.
 

Next Steps
 
8.   
Once agreed by the Lead Cabinet Member for Planning
at South Cambridgeshire District Council and the Cabinet Member for
Planning and Transport at Cambridge City Council, the Greater
Cambridge Housing Trajectory and Housing Land Supply document
(April 2026) will be published on the Councils’ shared
planning service website.

content:
The
purpose of this decision is to approve capital expenditure of
£135,000 to progress the next phase of the Council’s
LED lighting replacement programme, as outlined in the report
presented to Informal Cabinet on 10 March 2026.
This
phase focuses on converting remaining non?LED lighting assets
across the Council’s operational HQ site (South Cambs Hall)
to energy?efficient LED technology. The proposed works
will:

Deliver significant reductions in electricity consumption, with
projected efficiencies
of 70–80% compared with existing
luminaires.
Contribute to the Council’s carbon?reduction commitments
and sustainability objectives through lower energy use and
decreased maintenance requirements.
Improve lighting quality across buildings, enhancing the working
environment and long?term asset resilience.

Approval is now required to proceed with procurement and
delivery of the installations in accordance with the
Council’s financial and governance procedures.
 
This
decision has been considered previously by informal cabinet on
10/03/26.

To
proceed with the remaining Phase 2 LED lighting works at South
Cambs Hall.

This
decision is made to enable delivery of the projected energy
efficiencies, cost savings, and environmental benefits.

Option:  (Do Nothing)
Defer all Phase 2 activity
Reason for Rejection: To pause all Phase 2 LED replacement activity until after Local
Government Reorganisation (LGR) is complete.
Implications of this option:

No immediate expenditure
While deferring the programme would avoid capital outlay in the
short term, this does not remove the need for future investment.
The existing non?LED lighting stock continues to age and will still
require eventual replacement.
Lost opportunity for significant energy
savingsPostponing the programme
would delay realising the forecast 70–80% reduction in
electricity usage achievable through LED technology. This
represents a substantial missed opportunity for in?year revenue
savings and would prolong higher utility costs during a period of
increasing financial pressure.
Risk of cost
escalationDeferral may expose the
Council to higher installation and materials costs in future years
due to market inflation, supply chain pressures, and the ongoing
transition away from older lighting technologies. The overall
scheme could therefore become more expensive to
deliver.
Reduced contribution to carbon?reduction
goals
Continuing with inefficient lighting would delay progress against
corporate energy?reduction and sustainability targets, undermining
the Council’s wider environmental commitments.
Operational inefficiencies and increased
maintenance burden
Retaining outdated luminaires results in higher maintenance demand,
increased failure rates, and reduced lighting quality across the
operational estate.

 

Conclusion
This
option was rejected because, although it avoids immediate spend, it
results in higher operating costs, increased medium?term financial
risk, and delayed environmental benefits, with no strategic
advantages gained by postponing Phase 2.
topline: The Lead Cabinet Member for Environment has decided to approve £135,000 for the LED lighting replacement programme at South Cambs Hall.

The
purpose of this decision is to decide whether the land/building
nominated should be included as an asset of community value
(“ACV”) on the Council’s register of
ACVs.
 
On
26/01/2026 a nomination was received from Foxton Parish Council in
respect of Foxton Post Office and Stores, 38
High Street, Foxton, Cambridgeshire CB22 6RQ. This is a
re-nomination of an asset that is listed and due to expire on
05/04/2026.
 
 
Following consideration of the nomination, Notice of Nomination
was sent to Cllr James Hobro, (for the district Ward of Foxton), to
the Parish Council acknowledging their nomination and to the
owners, occupiers and Mortgage company. The nomination was
publicised through the Council’s parish e-bulletin and the
Lead Member for Communities was notified.

Officers have considered the nomination along with the feedback
received following issue of Notices of Nomination and are satisfied
that the non-ancillary and current use of the asset as detailed in
the nomination form and accompanying map does further the social
well-being, or cultural recreational or sporting interests of the
local community. It is also considered realistic to think there can
continue to be non-ancillary use of the asset which will further
the social interests of the local community. Therefore, it can be
accepted onto the Council’s list of Assets of Community
Value, in accordance with Section 88 (1) of the Localism Act
2011.

Foxton
Post Office and Stores provide clear and demonstrable social value
to the community of Foxton and the neighbouring
villages.
It acts
as a central point for information and notices, village survey
collection, fund raising activities and ticket sales for community
events.
The
store helps support a range of local activities including concerts
by the Foxton singers, the Pre-school Christmas box fundraiser, the
Scarecrow festival, open gardens and the Christmas window
fundraiser in aid of the church and schools.
A
coffee machine within the store offers residents a social meeting
place, helping them connect with each other and with staff, who
also support more vulnerable residents. The asset further
contributes to community wellbeing by receiving prescription
deliveries from local GP surgeries in Harston and Melbourn—an
essential service for Foxton’s significant number of older
residents and those unable to drive.
The
Post Office facilities are relied upon by local charities and
residents without access to transport, particularly for pension
collection and banking services.
The
store has offered work experience placements for young people,
helping to develop their skills and confidence. Younger children
are also able to visit the store independently in a safe and
supportive environment, enabling them to learn independence and
manage small purchases responsibly.
Additional support is provided through grocery deliveries to
some older residents, and staff in the Post Office assist
individuals who need help understanding digital messages or
processes.
 
Taken
together, these functions demonstrate that the asset’s
primary role significantly furthers the
social interests and social wellbeing of the local community and
therefore meets the definition of an Asset of Community
Value.

The
options are:
(a) To
accept the nomination and place the asset on the register of assets
of community value
(b) To
refuse the nomination and place the asset on the register of
unsuccessful nominations
topline: The Communications and Communities Service Manager has decided to include Foxton Post Office and Stores as an asset of community value on the Council's register.

content:
The committee received a full
application for the erection of a single self-build dwelling and
associated infrastructure and works.
 
The Senior
Planner provided the following updates since the publication of the
agenda:

i.              
The Local Highways Authority had no objections to
the revised drawing which reduced the width of the
access.

ii.             
Natural England had been consulted on the Site of
Specific Scientific Interest (SSSI) Assessment. No comments had
been received to date. Officers considered that the assessment was
acceptable and the development of one dwelling would not result in
significant recreational pressure upon the nearby
SSSI.

iii.            
The development was not of a scale which would
warrant consideration by the Design Panel.

iv.           
Amended the planning balance – Biodiversity
Net Gain has been added to the material considerations for approval
and the location of the residential dwelling outside the
development framework has been added to the material considerations
for refusal.

v.             
Proposed the deletion of condition 3 – which
was to secure the self-build element of the scheme and instead to
secure this through a legal agreement (Section 106 Unilateral
Undertaking) following recent Planning Inspector decisions which
did not consider that a condition to secure this was
appropriate.

vi.           
Amended the officer recommendation – to
approve the application subject to the conditions contained in the
officer report, with the deletion of condition 3 and to delegate
authority to officers to complete a legal agreement (Section 106
Unilateral Undertaking) to secure the self-build element of the
application.
 
In response to
members’ questions:
       
i.      
The Senior Planner commented that officer’s
view was that the proposed development was not inappropriate
development in the Green Belt; therefore, there would only be
limited harm to the character and appearance of the Green
Belt.
      
ii.       
The Delivery Manager further confirmed that in
officer’s opinion the development fulfilled the criteria for
Grey Belt land because there was a demonstrable unmet need for the
type of development proposed (a self-build
dwelling).
The committee
heard from Jeanette Vivier speaking in objection to the
application.
 
The
committee heard from Councillor Brian Milnes (Sawston Ward Member)
speaking as a local district member in support of the
application.
 
During debate
the Committee considered the following issues:

       
i.      
The proposal was in a sustainable location, but a
member objected to the term ‘Grey Belt’ land but noted
that this was a term used in National Planning
Policy.

      
ii.       
Although the site was outside the development
framework, looking at the character of the area, it was a piece of
green space within a built-up area.

    
iii.      
The application was a self-build application for one
single storey dwelling.

    
iv.      
The design of the dwelling would fit in with the
setting of the area.  

     
v.      
The Senior Planner’s advice around the weight
to be given to ‘Green Belt’ land and that this had
changed since the Planning Inspector’s appeal
decision.

    
vi.      
There would be limited impact on
neighbours.

   
vii.       
The width of the access into the site had been
reduced.

 
viii.      
Ecological concerns would be secured through a
planning condition.

    
ix.      
There was no public access to the
SSSI.
 
The Delivery Manager
summarised the amended officer recommendation to approve the
application subject to:
       
i.      
The conditions set out in the
officer’s report; with the deletion of condition 3 and
delegated authority for officers to make minor amendments to the
conditions as drafted; and
      
ii.       
The completion of a Section 106
Unilateral Undertaking to secure the self-build element of the
scheme.
 
By 8 votes in favour
(Councillors Anna Bradnam, Ariel Cahn, Martin Cahn, Corinne Garvie,
Lisa Redrup, Peter Sandford, Eileen Wilson, Heather Williams), 0
votes against and 1 abstention (Councillor Richard Williams), the
Committee approved the application subject to:

·      
The conditions set out in the officer’s
report; with the deletion of condition 3 and delegated authority
for officers to make minor amendments to the conditions as drafted;
and

·      
The completion of a Section 106 Unilateral
Undertaking to secure the self-build element of the
scheme.
topline: The Committee has decided to approve the application for a single self-build dwelling in a sustainable location.

content:

agenda:

the inclusion of additional landscape planting along the driveway

officers to complete a legal agreement (Section 106 Unilateral
Undertaking) to secure the self-build element of the
application.

members’ questions:
       
i.      
The Delivery Manager advised that following feedback
from recent Planning Inspector decisions the decision had been
taken to secure self / custom build development by a legal planning
agreement going forward rather than through a planning
condition.  This would apply to all
self/custom build applications coming forward.
      
ii.       
The Senior Planner advised that if the development
was approved both sites would have sufficient sized external
amenity space which would be in accordance with the District Design
Guide.
    
iii.      
The Senior Planner advised that the impact of the
proposed development on trees on the site would be assessed at
reserved matters stage once the siting and location of the dwelling
was confirmed. A condition requesting information about the impact
on trees was proposed.  
    
iv.      
The Delivery Manager confirmed that work was being
undertaken by officers to provide anecdotal information about how
many people on the self-build register were still actively seeking
self-build accommodation. 
The
Chair referred members to a written statement from the applicant in
support of the application, which had been published on the
council’s website in advance of the
meeting.
 
During debate
the Committee considered the following issues:

       
i.      
Welcomed the self-build application and noted the
applicant had said in their written statement that they wanted to
live in the proposed dwelling.

      
ii.       
The proposed development would replace the garages
with a more visually attractive development.

    
iii.      
Although the proposed development was outside the
development framework; it would be on Brownfield
land.

    
iv.      
Referred to comments from the Parish Council and
noted their request for native planting along the entrance
driveway. 
 
The Delivery Manager
summarised the amended officer recommendation to approve the
application subject to:

       
i.      
The conditions set out in the
officer’s report; with the deletion of condition 9 and
delegated authority for officers to make minor amendments to the
conditions as drafted; and

      
ii.       
An additional informative regarding
landscaping stating that the applicant is encouraged to consider
the inclusion of additional landscape planting along the driveway
through their soft landscaping scheme (condition 8);
and 

    
iii.      
Delegated authority to officers to
complete a Section 106 Unilateral Undertaking to secure the
self-build element of the application.
 
By unanimous vote of 8 vote,
the Committee approved the application subject to:

The
conditions set out in the officer’s report; with the deletion
of condition 9 and delegated authority for officers to make minor
amendments to the conditions as drafted.


·      
An additional informative regarding landscaping
stating that the applicant is encouraged to consider the inclusion
of additional landscape planting along the driveway through their
soft landscaping scheme (condition 8); and

·      
Delegated authority to officers to complete a
Section 106 Unilateral Undertaking to secure the self-build element
of the application.

purpose:
To
accept additional funding from the LAHF (Local Authority Housing
Fund) of £1,198,620 and agree to use this money, together
with borrowing, to purchase 6 additional homes.  These will initially be used for two purposes, 2
properties to accommodate refugees from a recognised scheme and 4
properties to be used for temporary accommodation. In the longer
term these will all revert to general needs HRA housing
stock.
 
It is a
condition of funding that two of the properties acquired under this
scheme are initially used to rehouse people who are refugees from a
recognised government scheme. The Council will ask the Strategic
Migration Partnership, or other similar agencies, for nominations
for these homes.
 
As
properties become available, if there are no eligible refugees at
that time, and to avoid properties remaining empty, it is proposed
to give the Head of Housing authority to use the property for wider
housing needs on either a temporary basis or to substitute with a
council property at a later stage.  The
latter option will only be considered in exceptional
circumstances.
 
The
properties that are for temporary accommodation will be let
directly by the Housing Needs team to reduce the use of expensive
temporary bed & breakfast accommodation, and to avoid placing
families in unsuitable accommodation,   
 
Although the properties acquired under this scheme are initially
for use by refugees or as temporary accommodation, in the longer
term the properties will be part of the HRA general needs housing
stock.  It is proposed to give power to
the Head of Housing to determine when each property transfers to
general needs use but this determination needs to take account of
the housing needs of refugees and demand for temporary
accommodation.
 
The
Council has previously received around £ 14.5m to purchase 85
homes under previous rounds of LAHF funding.

content:
The purpose of this decision is
to seek agreement for the adoption of the Bourn Conservation
Area Appraisal and Management Plan.

Accept the recommendations and approve the Bourn
Conservation Area Appraisal.

The preparation and adoption of the Bourn CAAMP document
is consistent with the discharge of the statutory obligations of
the Council as LPA for these areas. The process followed in the
preparation of the plans included consultation and engagement and I
am satisfied that the resultant plans have fully considered the
representations made and are necessary for the effective
preservation and enhancement of the Conservation Area of Bourn.

There is the possibility to adopt, or not to
adopt, the appraisal. With respect to the boundary changes, the
options are to leave the conservation area boundary unchanged as
recommended, or to make changes to the boundary which are different
from those recommended.

support for the preferred approach and therefore the other options
are not being taken forward.

content:
The
Council voted (unanimous) on the motion by Councillor Helene
Leeming, which was carried as follows:
 
“Council notes:

Cambridgeshire, and in particular South Cambridgeshire, has seen
rapid population growth over recent years. This has resulted in
greater demand on services that are important to our residents such
as policing, fire and rescue, education, healthcare and
more.
Government has been working on plans to accelerate this growth,
most recently proposing that a Development Corporation be
established.
Cambridgeshire’s population is expected to grow to
1,078,000 by 2041.
Government funding for many of these key services in
Cambridgeshire significantly lags behind other areas.

 
Council
notes, as an example, Cambridgeshire Police:

Cambridgeshire Police is the 4th worst funded police force in
the country on a per person basis. Were the force to receive the
average national funding per person in 2025/26., it would have an
additional £28 million a year in funding.
To
maintain existing policing levels as the population increases,
Cambridgeshire Police will need to recruit an additional 17
officers per year between now and 2041.
The
formula used to determine funding for police forces is still based
on 2011 Census data, despite it now being 2026.

 
Council
notes, as a further example, education funding:

The
f40 fairer funding campaign, which provides comparative historical
data, has exposed huge variations in funding allocations per pupil
by local authority.
For
funding per pupil, Cambridgeshire remains in the bottom quartile
nationally for the dedicated schools grant and for the high needs
block funding per pupil. In 2025/26, Cambridgeshire ranked 133rd
out of 151 local authorities.
If
Cambridgeshire received equivalent funding per pupil to
Lincolnshire, near the national median, we would receive an
additional £23.8 million a year. If Cambridgeshire received
equivalent funding per pupil to Peterborough, it would receive an
additional £33 million a year.

 
Council
believes:

The
failure of Government to adequately fund key services across
Cambridgeshire, especially in light of their ambitions for growth
in our area, is unacceptable, has negatively impacted our residents
and cannot continue.

 
Council
resolves:
·      
To request that the Leader write to the Home
Secretary, the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and
Local Government and other relevant ministers expressing our
frustration at the Government’s chronic underfunding of key
services in our county and imploring ministers to review how
funding for these services is allocated, recognising the scale of
growth across the Greater Cambridge area.”
topline: The Council has decided to address chronic underfunding of key services in Cambridgeshire due to rapid population growth.
